body_markdown:
Ask a program sponsor how many sites are ready for construction, and the honest answer is often “give us a few weeks.” Not because the number is hard to calculate. Because nobody budgeted the time, or gave anyone the job, of calculating it fast.


This isn’t a scheduling problem in the usual sense. Nobody is dragging their feet. It’s a structural problem: the baseline sits on the schedule as a milestone, with a date by which it’s supposed to be locked, but it doesn’t sit anywhere on the budget as a funded task. The work is assumed to happen as overhead, done by whoever’s available, squeezed in around their actual job.


### The cost shows up as delay, not as a missed step


Nothing about this looks broken in the moment. The baseline milestone passes, someone starts pulling the record together, and the program moves on assuming it’ll catch up. It doesn’t cause a problem today. It sits, half-assembled, until a permitting deadline or a capital approval needs a number nobody has ready – and by then, “give us a few weeks” has become the answer to everything downstream too.


Ask most program managers how this gets caught earlier and the honest answer is usually a person. Someone pulling exports from leasing, network, and ops, and reconciling the conflicts by hand – the site marked active in one system and decommissioned in another, the equipment count that doesn’t match the last truck roll. That works, for a handful of sites. It doesn’t scale to a portfolio.


### No Budget Line, No Milestone


The instinct is often to fix this with better project management: a firmer deadline, a more disciplined check-in, a spreadsheet someone owns and updates by hand. Those help at the margins. They don’t solve the underlying issue, which is that the baseline was never treated as real work with a real cost – it was treated as something that happens between the real line items.


A milestone with no funded task behind it isn’t a commitment. It’s hope with a date on it.


### What closes the gap


The fix isn’t asking anyone to work faster under the same conditions. It’s recognizing the baseline as its own piece of work, funded and owned like any other deliverable, backed by a record that’s reconciled continuously instead of assembled from scratch every time someone asks. When the estate record is already current, the six-week question becomes a same-day one – because the answer exists before anyone has to go looking for it.


### Where we come in


This is what Sitenna’s Management Cloud is built to solve: a single, continuously reconciled record across leasing, network, and field status, so a baseline doesn’t have to be rebuilt by hand every time a program needs one. Instead of a person assembling the answer under pressure, the record stays current in the background, ready the moment a sponsor, a regulator, or a capital planning cycle asks for it.
